blocks.html: These three goads here were in truth very sharp ones, to bring a man back from a distant country: namely, the sweetness of one's native land, the tender love of one's children, and the love of one's wife. For as to one's native land, one could scarcely express (says Cicero in some place) what sweetness, what pleasure, what love and delight it contains a; which, being infinitely great, brings it about that another country, though it be more beautiful, pleasant and fertile, will nevertheless never be found so gracious or so delectable b2. Witness Ulysses, who of old dared well to prefer Ithaca (where he was born), stony, set like a little nest among the rough rocks and almost inaccessible, to the immortality that Calypso the nymph had offered him c2. On which subject Ovid says q,

notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon qu'il eut ad Quiri tes poſt reditũ.
notes.gloss: Cicero's speech to the people on his return from exile, on the sweetness of one's native land.

notes.gloss: Cicero: the wisest of men preferred Ithaca, "fixed like a little nest upon the roughest of rocks," to immortality — the words Coras paraphrases.
Nescio qua natale solum dulcedine cunctos / ducit et immemores non sinit esse sui — the couplet translated in the text.

blocks.html: By I know not what sweetness the native soil draws all men, and does not suffer them to be unmindful of it.

Of paternal affection toward the child, there is no one who does not know (or he would be more felonious, brutal and unnatural than the beasts) that it is exceedingly great, even to surmounting the love that each one bears to himself. Wherefore Virgil, speaking of Aeneas and of Ascanius his son, did not say without cause e,

notes.gloss: Omnis in Ascanio cari stat cura parentis — the line translated in the text.

blocks.html: All the care of the loving father rests upon Ascanius.

And King David, although he had been outrageously and in several ways offended by his son Absalom, both because he had caused Amnon his other son to be killed, and afterwards abused his concubines, and also because he had plotted his death, nevertheless, when David heard that the head of Absalom his son had been caught by an oak, and he left hanging there, could not contain himself from crying out and saying thus: My SON Absalom, my son, my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee, Absalom my son, my son <sup class="mk" data-key="f" data-page="p032">f</sup>. And touching conjugal love, everyone is sufficiently persuaded, with Propertius <sup class="mk" data-key="g" data-page="p032">g</sup>, that it surmounts all the others.

notes.original: Au liure ij. des Rois cha. xiij. xvi. xvij. & xviii.
notes.gloss: The murder of Amnon (13), Absalom and David's concubines (16), the plot against David's life (17), Absalom caught by the head in the oak and David's lament, 18:9 and 18:33.

notes.original: Properce au iiii. des Ele gies.
notes.gloss: Omnis amor magnus, sed aperto in coniuge maior — the line translated in the text; Arethusa to Lycotas. Coras's print reads apertè.

blocks.html: All love is great, but plainly greater in a spouse.

Whereof, among infinite others, Pericles the Athenian could well answer, who so loved Aspasia his wife that he would never leave her, nor go out of his house, at whatever hour it might be, without having first kissed her <sup class="mk" data-key="h" data-page="p032">h</sup>. I leave aside Periander of Corinth, who loved his wife so madly that he had to do with her when she was quite dead; and Orpheus, who did indeed venture (as the poets relate) to go down to the underworld to ask for his wife, whom a serpent had killed, and did so much that Pluto <sup class="mk" data-key="i" data-page="p032">i</sup> and Proserpina gave her back to him, on a condition, however, which afterwards, out of impatience of love, he could not keep.

notes.original: Plutarque en la vie de Pericles.
notes.gloss: Pericles kissed Aspasia every day on going out and coming home.

notes.citation: Virgil, Georgics IV.453–527; Ovid, Metamorphoses X.1–85 (the book number is dropped in the print)
notes.original: vergile. au iiij. des Georgiques, & Oui de aux de la Metarmorphoſe.
notes.gloss: Orpheus and Eurydice; the condition that he not look back. The Periander story (Herodotus V.92) carries no citation.
